one_liner: Apache Thrift's C++ binary protocol: IDL-generated structs, fixed-width encoding; ~2.2x faster than msgpack-c in one round-trip test.
what_it_does: Thrift is Apache's cross-language RPC and serialization stack (28 languages). You describe types in a .thrift IDL file, and the thrift compiler generates C++ structs with read(TProtocol*) and write(TProtocol*) methods. You pair those with a protocol (TBinaryProtocol, TCompactProtocol, JSON) and a transport (TMemoryBuffer for in-memory bytes, or sockets and HTTP for RPC). For plain serialization you wrap a TMemoryBuffer in TBinaryProtocolT<TMemoryBuffer>, call obj.write(&proto), and take the bytes out with getBufferAsString(). This is a different API and wire format from MessagePack, not a drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: The binary protocol writes every integer at fixed width in big-endian order (an i64 is a byte swap plus 8 bytes) and every string as a 4-byte length plus raw bytes, so encoding and decoding need no varint branches. TBinaryProtocolT is a template over the transport, so with TMemoryBuffer each field goes through TBufferBase's inline fast path: one bounds check and one memcpy. readStringBody() borrow()s the string straight from the buffer and assigns it, and the generated read() fills the typed struct directly, reusing the destination vectors' capacity. The msgpack-c path in the same harness unpacks into an intermediate msgpack::object tree and then convert()s it into the struct.
when_to_use: You already have a Thrift IDL, or want one schema shared across C++ and other languages, and need fast round trips of C++ structs through in-memory buffers (cache blobs, queue payloads, stored records).
Records dominated by int64 arrays and medium-length strings, where CPU time matters more than bytes on the wire.
Hot loops that can reuse one TMemoryBuffer, one protocol object and one destination struct across calls, which is how the benchmark ran it.
You may later want RPC on the same types: the generated code and protocols plug into Thrift's client/server stack.
when_not_to_use: Size-sensitive storage or network links: the binary encoding was 17,017 B against msgpack's 13,402 B (~27% larger) in this test. TCompactProtocol is smaller (13,378 B) but took 3474 ms in the same run, slower than both msgpack and protobuf.
Schemaless or dynamic data, or data that arbitrary tools must read without an IDL. MessagePack is self-describing; Thrift binary is not.
Maximum raw C++ speed: in the same shootout cereal (1052 ms) and YAS (303 ms) were faster, and Cap'n Proto and FlatBuffers took 401 and 492 ms for a full build, serialize and deserialize cycle.

Untrusted input on older releases: 0.24.0 fixes C++ issues including CVE-2026-55969 (integer overflow in container size prechecks) and CVE-2026-55970 (heap over-read in THeaderTransport). Stay on a current release.
You want a small header-only dependency: this needs a built libthrift plus the thrift compiler in your build.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (libthrift, chosen with CMake BUILD_SHARED_LIBS) plus the thrift code generator at build time
integration.dependencies: thrift compiler for code generation; libthrift links pthreads and librt, with OpenSSL for the SSL sockets (the CMake build skips SSL if OpenSSL is absent or disabled); Boost headers to build (TUuid is implemented on boost::uuids; Boost is not a runtime link dependency); libevent only for libthriftnb (non-blocking server); zlib only for thriftz
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMake default CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); C++03/C++98 dropped after 0.12.0. The benchmark built Thrift 0.12.0 with C++14.
integration.platforms: Linux and other POSIX systems, Windows 7 or later (XP/Vista dropped after 0.12.0); byte order is fixed by the protocol (TNetworkBigEndian default, TLEBinaryProtocol for little-endian), so no architecture requirement is documented
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for protocol and buffer objects. TMemoryBuffer and TBinaryProtocolT hold mutable read/write cursors, so give each thread its own instances.

gotchas: Generated code takes TProtocol* by default, so each readI64/readString call is a virtual dispatch into the templated protocol. `thrift --gen cpp:templates` generates templatized reader/writer methods instead. The benchmark used the default, non-templated output.

TBinaryProtocol's string and container size limits default to 0 (unlimited); only TConfiguration's max message size (100 MB default) bounds what a hostile length prefix can make it allocate. Call setStringSizeLimit/setContainerSizeLimit for untrusted data.
TMemoryBuffer::resetBuffer(buf, sz) defaults to the OBSERVE policy: it reads your memory in place without copying, so that memory must outlive the parse.
Fields marked `required` in the IDL make read() throw TProtocolException(INVALID_DATA) when absent, which limits later schema changes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Thrift over cereal or Boost.Serialization when the same schema must be read from other languages or later carried over RPC; those two are C++-only. For C++-only data in this same test, cereal was a bit faster (1052 vs 1190 ms), is header-only and needs no IDL, and Boost.Serialization was a tie (1195 ms).
verified_claims_summary: In the third-party thekvs/cpp-serializers shootout (2019 README table: Thrift 0.12.0, msgpack-c 3.1.1, protobuf 3.7.0; C++14 CMake Release build, compiler unnamed in the current README; 'Intel Core i7', Ubuntu 16.04), round-tripping one ~17 KB record (1,000 int64 values plus 100 86-char strings) through TBinaryProtocolT<TMemoryBuffer> took 1190.22 ms in total, against 2560.6 ms for msgpack (~2.15x) and 2312.78 ms for protobuf (~1.94x). The Thrift loop even includes a copy of the output into a std::string each iteration. The stated 1,000,000 iterations would mean ~1.2 us per round trip, which looks too fast, so trust the ratios rather than the absolute times.
status_note: Actively maintained Apache-2.0 project (v0.24.0 released 2026-07-11, commits through 2026-09-24), but the only speed evidence is for 0.12.0 from 2019, so the current release has not been measured.
